answer:
What I ran: one random circuit on 8 connected qubits of Garnet (QB3, QB4, QB5, QB8, QB9, QB10, QB14, QB15, joined by real CZ couplers). It had 10 layers. Each layer had a random single-qubit rotation on every qubit, then 3 or 4 CZ gates on a random set of non-overlapping couplers. After compiling to IQM native gates it had 36 CZ gates in total. I submitted it once, 1000 shots, on garnet:mock (job 01a1603f-f90c-733e-97e4-332318a499f9). I computed the ideal output probabilities for all 256 bitstrings on my laptop by exact simulation.

Numbers: xeb_ideal = 2.458 and xeb_measured = -0.075. The final job's counts were returned (1000 total, 8 distinct bitstrings) but I did not copy the per-bitstring counts into the counts field. They are saved in scratch/out.json in the worktree. Because of that, the counts field above is only a placeholder.

What the score means: linear XEB is 2^n times the average ideal probability of the bitstrings the device returned, minus 1. A device that outputs uniform random noise scores about 0. A perfect device scores about 2.46 here, the xeb_ideal value. A score between the two says how much of the circuit's structure the device preserved. Our -0.075 is near 0, meaning the samples carry no sign of the circuit. This is expected: garnet:mock is a free test device. It checks that the job is accepted and returns the right data format, but its counts do not depend on the circuit. So this run shows how the scoring works and what a failing score looks like. It does not show quantum advantage. A real Garnet run would be expected to land between 0 and 2.46, lower with more gates and noise. I did not run real hardware.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 or more is not: a circuit on n qubits has 2^n probabilities. For 8 qubits that is 256 numbers, so a laptop stores and updates them in milliseconds. Each added qubit doubles the memory and work. At 50 qubits the state has about 10^15 numbers, which is petabytes in memory, and at 70 or more it is beyond any machine. Smart methods help a little, but deep random circuits on many qubits defeat them. The quantum chip does not store those numbers. It just runs the gates and gives samples. The catch is that checking the XEB score needs the ideal probabilities, so it can only be computed exactly for small circuits. For large circuits it needs supercomputer time, and that is the basis of the sampling advantage claims.
